job.style: a passage that shows a common wrong method and corrects it

response.passage: When plotting a linear relation on a Cartesian plane, students often make mistakes by misunderstanding the axes. Some think the origin is simply the bottom-left corner of the grid, but it is actually the intersection where the x-axis and y-axis meet at (0,0). Another common error occurs when plotting coordinates like (1, 4). A student might mistakenly count 4 units up and 1 unit across, forgetting that the first number represents the x-coordinate, which dictates horizontal movement from the origin. Furthermore, when drawing a linear graph, some students incorrectly believe the line should stop exactly at the last plotted point. In reality, a linear relation represents a continuous pattern, so the line must extend beyond the plotted points to show it continues infinitely. Finally, when connecting points, some students try to draw a wavy curve through them. This is incorrect; because the relation is linear, you must use a straight edge to draw a single straight line that passes through all the points. By following these rules—starting from the origin, correctly identifying coordinates, and extending straight lines—you can accurately represent mathematical relationships on a graph.
response.summary: This passage explains how to correctly plot points and draw linear graphs on a Cartesian plane. It clarifies the position of the origin, the order of coordinates, and the necessity of extending straight lines.
